name: Introduction to Communication
description: A foundational course introducing students to the nature, functions, and contexts of human communication from self-concept to public speaking and digital media.

modules.title: What is Communication
modules.objectives: Define communication and explain its core components; identify the levels of communication and why studying communication matters. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, the communication process: Diagram sender, receiver, message, channel, feedback, and noise; contrast linear, interaction, and transaction models using the deadline case.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 1: What is Communication. Focus: Define communication and explain its core components; identify the levels of communication and why studying communication matters. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Label the components and two forms of noise in the fictional deadline case, then draft a clearer message and confirmation reply.
modules.assignment: Fictional case (all people and events are invented): On Thursday at 4:00 p.m., Maya posts in the project group chat: “Send me your slides by Friday night. I’ll upload everything after dinner.” The teacher’s actual deadline is Friday at 6:00 p.m., but Maya does not include it. Leo reads the message and interprets “Friday night” as 9:00 p.m. He replies, “I’ll send mine at nine tomorrow.” Priya interprets it as before Maya’s dinner, around 5:00 p.m. Priya asks, “Do you mean five tomorrow, before dinner?” A network outage delays Priya’s question until Saturday. Maya replies to Leo on Thursday, “Okay, thanks,” without noticing the proposed time or clarifying the deadline. On Friday Priya sends her slides at 5:00 p.m.; Leo sends his at 9:00 p.m.; Maya uploads the project at 9:15 p.m., after the teacher’s deadline. Submit: a 250-word analysis. Include: sender, receivers, channel, the actual message, and the feedback exchange; identify at least two distinct forms of noise using evidence from the case (ambiguous wording and disrupted message delivery). Explain how each interferes with understanding or coordination. Then rewrite Maya’s message with the deadline and individual responsibilities and provide a confirmation reply that closes the feedback loop. Evaluation: correct use of the communication model, specific scenario evidence for two distinct noise mechanisms, and a practical revision that checks shared understanding.

modules.title: Types & Functions of Communication
modules.objectives: Distinguish among intrapersonal, interpersonal, small group, public, and mass communication; describe the social, instrumental, and identity functions of communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, communication history and forms: Compare intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public, and mass communication; classify your five fictional scenarios and justify each level. Connect each to an instrumental, relational, or identity goal using the lesson.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 2: Types & Functions of Communication. Focus: Distinguish among intrapersonal, interpersonal, small group, public, and mass communication; describe the social, instrumental, and identity functions of communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Classify five invented school-safe scenarios by communication level and function, with a clue for each choice.
modules.assignment: Use five provided or invented school-safe scenarios rather than recording private interactions. Submit: a chart and a 200-word comparison. Include: the communication level, primary function, channel, intended audience, and one quoted or described clue for each classification. Evaluation: accurate classifications, clear evidence for each choice, and one supported pattern across the five cases.

modules.title: Self-Concept & Communication
modules.objectives: Explain how self-concept and self-esteem develop and influence communication behavior; apply the looking-glass self concept. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, perceiving and presenting self: Read the self-concept, self-esteem, reflected appraisal, and social comparison discussions. Mark coach, teacher, and peer evidence in Mina’s case and distinguish perceived judgments from established facts.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 3: Self-Concept & Communication. Focus: Explain how self-concept and self-esteem develop and influence communication behavior; apply the looking-glass self concept. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Create a ten-word self-concept inventory for fictional Mina and connect two labels to perceived feedback. A fictional alternative is allowed; private information need not be submitted.
modules.assignment: Fictional source material: Mina’s coach says, “You explain drills clearly, but you hesitate to lead the warm-up.” Her teacher says, “Your written explanations are careful; I would like to hear your ideas in class.” Her peer Jo says, “You always get nervous, so I should present instead.” Mina thinks, “If Jo sees me as a poor speaker, maybe I am one.” She compares herself with teammate Ren, who speaks without notes, and stops volunteering even though she prepares detailed notes. These are fictional observations, not diagnoses. Analyze a fictional vignette in which a student receives conflicting feedback from a coach, a teacher, and a peer. Submit: a 350-word case analysis. Include: two examples of reflected appraisal, one social comparison, one possible effect on communication behavior, and a supportive response that avoids stereotyping. Evaluation: accurate use of self-concept concepts, evidence from the vignette, and respectful reasoning. No personal disclosure is required.

modules.title: Verbal Messages
modules.objectives: Analyze how word choice, language style, and denotative versus connotative meaning affect communication outcomes. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, language and meaning: Distinguish denotation from connotation and examine abstraction and context; annotate your chosen public text for word choices and revise ambiguous wording using evidence.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 4: Verbal Messages. Focus: Analyze how word choice, language style, and denotative versus connotative meaning affect communication outcomes. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Draft five ambiguous sentences for a fictional school announcement and rewrite each to clarify the intended meaning.
modules.assignment: Select a political speech, advertisement, or public announcement and analyze it in 350 words: identify examples of connotative language, euphemisms, and either inclusive or exclusive language. Explain how each specific word choice likely shapes the audience's perception of the message. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: drafts, annotations, quotations, analysis, or revised writing from the Verbal Messages module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Nonverbal Messages
modules.objectives: Identify and categorize types of nonverbal communication; explain how nonverbal cues complement, contradict, and regulate verbal communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, principles and functions of nonverbal communication: Identify nonverbal channels and functions, including regulating, complementing, and contradicting verbal messages; explain how context changes interpretations in the five fictional descriptions.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 5: Nonverbal Messages. Focus: Identify and categorize types of nonverbal communication; explain how nonverbal cues complement, contradict, and regulate verbal communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are (TED Talk) Focus: Identify and categorize types of nonverbal communication; explain how nonverbal cues complement, contradict, and regulate verbal communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Classify the five embedded nonverbal descriptions by channel and likely function; add one alternative interpretation for each.
modules.assignment: Fictional source material: (1) In class, a student raises a hand and the teacher gives them the next turn. (2) In a workplace meeting, a colleague steps back when another person moves very close. (3) In an online meeting, a speaker says “I am fine” with a trembling voice and long pauses. (4) At school, a student looks away while silently considering a difficult question. (5) In a workplace video call, a colleague sits upright and nods as a new task is explained. Analyze plausible functions rather than treating any behavior as proof of an emotion or intention. Analyze five provided descriptions of nonverbal behavior in school, workplace, and online-meeting settings. Submit: a table and a 200-word conclusion. Include: the channel (facial expression, gesture, eye behavior, posture, touch, space, or vocalics), likely function, scenario evidence, and one contextual factor that could change the meaning of each cue. Evaluation: accurate categories, evidence-based reasoning, attention to context, and avoidance of claims that a cue has one universal meaning. No experiment on other people is required.

modules.title: Listening Skills
modules.objectives: Differentiate types of listening; apply active listening strategies to improve comprehension and relational quality in conversations. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, barriers to effective listening: Identify distraction, response preparation, interruption, and prejudgment as barriers; annotate the fictional transcript and use the lesson’s HURIER framework to plan revised responses.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 6: Listening Skills. Focus: Differentiate types of listening; apply active listening strategies to improve comprehension and relational quality in conversations. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — 5 Ways to Listen Better (TED Talk) Focus: Differentiate types of listening; apply active listening strategies to improve comprehension and relational quality in conversations. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Apply each HURIER step to the fictional Ari–Bea transcript and rewrite four barrier-producing replies; no private partner transcript is needed.
modules.assignment: Fictional source material: Transcript: Ari: “The project deadline moved from Friday to Thursday, and I need help with the chart.” Bea, scrolling on a phone: “Sorry, I was reading messages. What date?” Ari: “Thursday. I am worried about checking the data.” Bea, interrupting before Ari finishes: “Just use last week’s chart.” Ari: “Those numbers changed.” Bea: “I am already planning how to defend our old chart, so I missed what changed.” Ari: “Can I explain the new totals?” Bea: “You always worry, so I do not need to hear the details.” Barriers to annotate are distraction, interruption, rehearsing a response, and prejudging the speaker. Use a provided fictional conversation transcript. Submit: an annotated copy and a 250-word reflection. Include: four marked listening barriers, four revised responses using paraphrasing, clarifying questions, or perception checks, and a brief explanation of why each revision is more effective. Evaluation: accurate identification of barriers, responses that preserve the speaker’s meaning, and clear links to active-listening principles. No private conversation log is required.

modules.title: Interpersonal Relationships
modules.objectives: Describe stages of relationship development and dissolution; explain how trust, commitment, and communication patterns shape interpersonal relationships. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, foundations of relationships: Read relationship development and maintenance, especially Knapp’s stages; match the fictional friendship events to stage evidence and explain why progression need not be fixed.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 7: Interpersonal Relationships. Focus: Describe stages of relationship development and dissolution; explain how trust, commitment, and communication patterns shape interpersonal relationships. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — What Makes a Good Conversation (TED) Focus: Describe stages of relationship development and dissolution; explain how trust, commitment, and communication patterns shape interpersonal relationships. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Map fictional Eli and Sam’s relationship events onto Knapp’s model and explain one model limitation. A fictional alternative is allowed; private information need not be submitted.
modules.assignment: Fictional source material: At a school club, Eli introduces themself to Sam: “Hi, I am new here.” The next week Sam asks, “Which games do you enjoy?” They exchange low-risk hobby details. A month later Eli says, “I get nervous presenting; could we rehearse together?” Sam agrees and keeps the conversation private. They begin meeting each week, share more concerns, and say, “I trust you to tell me when my explanation is unclear.” At the current endpoint, they describe themselves as friends but keep separate activities and have made no public formal commitment. Use the recent greater disclosure and time together to justify intensifying; explain any defensible alternative stage label. Apply Knapp’s Relationship Model to a provided fictional friendship or mentorship case. Submit: a 350-word analysis. Include: the current stage, two quoted or paraphrased communication events as evidence, an explanation of how those events changed the relationship, and one limitation of applying a stage model to real relationships. Evaluation: accurate stage evidence, careful reasoning, and recognition that relationships may not follow a fixed sequence. No personal relationship disclosure is required.

modules.title: Conflict in Communication
modules.objectives: Identify sources and styles of interpersonal conflict; apply constructive communication strategies to manage and resolve conflict. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenWA Communication Studies, conflict and interpersonal communication: Distinguish conflict sources and avoiding, accommodating, competing, compromising, and collaborating styles. Apply I-statements and listening checks to Noor and Kai’s deadline conflict.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 8: Conflict in Communication. Focus: Identify sources and styles of interpersonal conflict; apply constructive communication strategies to manage and resolve conflict. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment. Apply the relevant concepts to the module’s assignment and explain one example in your own words.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — Classify the initial conflict styles in the Noor–Kai case and draft two I-statements plus a collaborative agreement. A fictional alternative is allowed; private information need not be submitted.
modules.assignment: Fictional source material: For a shared school project, Noor believed the team’s draft was due at 6 p.m.; Kai understood 8 p.m. The teacher’s final deadline is 9 p.m. Noor needs an hour to assemble slides; Kai needs time to verify a chart. Noor says, “You always ruin our projects. Upload it now or I will remove your name.” Kai says, “Fine, I will not talk about it anymore,” closes the chat, and stops responding. Twenty minutes later Kai returns and explains the chart concern. Neither had confirmed the internal deadline. Analyze Noor’s initial competing style and Kai’s initial avoiding response, then propose an agreement addressing both needs. Analyze a provided fictional conflict about a shared project deadline. Submit: a 400-word case response. Include: the conflict source, each party’s conflict style, two quoted lines that escalate the conflict, revised I-statements and listening responses, and a proposed agreement. Evaluation: accurate conflict concepts, specific textual evidence, and a workable de-escalation plan. No personal conflict disclosure is required.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the basic communication process?
options: Sender
Channel
Receiver
Profit motive
quizQuestions.answer: Profit motive
quizQuestions.explanation: The basic communication process consists of sender, message, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver, feedback, and noise. Profit motive is not a component.

quizQuestions.question: Communication competence refers to:
options: Communicating effectively and appropriately in context
Speaking confidently regardless of audience expectations
Using several languages with accurate pronunciation
Following grammar rules without considering social context
quizQuestions.answer: Communicating effectively and appropriately in context
quizQuestions.explanation: Communication competence means knowing what communication behaviors are effective and appropriate for a given context and being able to perform them.

quizQuestions.question: In the communication process, noise is best defined as:
options: The meaning a sender intends to convey
The receiver’s reply to the original message
The medium used to carry the message
Interference with message creation or meaning
quizQuestions.answer: Interference with message creation or meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: Noise may be physical, psychological, semantic, or technical and can disrupt meaning at several points.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Studying communication is valuable because.
quizQuestions.answer: Studying communication helps people build stronger relationships, solve problems, and participate more effectively in school, work, and civic life.
quizQuestions.explanation: Communication study matters because it improves practical choices in relationships, teamwork, public speaking, and everyday problem solving.

quizQuestions.question: Which level of communication involves only one person engaged in internal thought and self-talk?
options: Intrapersonal communication
Interpersonal communication
Small group communication
Public communication
quizQuestions.answer: Intrapersonal communication
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication occurs within an individual — the internal dialogue and self-reflection that takes place in one's own mind.

quizQuestions.question: The instrumental function of communication refers to using communication to:
options: Maintain relationships through greetings and emotional support
Achieve practical goals and get things done
Define personal identity through stories about yourself
Entertain others through humor and playful conversation
quizQuestions.answer: Achieve practical goals and get things done
quizQuestions.explanation: The instrumental function of communication involves using messages to accomplish tasks, make requests, or achieve practical objectives.

quizQuestions.question: Mass communication is distinguished from other forms primarily by:
options: Exchanging personal messages within a small private group
Sharing ideas between two people in a conversation
Addressing a small audience gathered in one room
Reaching large, diverse audiences through media
quizQuestions.answer: Reaching large, diverse audiences through media
quizQuestions.explanation: Mass communication transmits messages to large, heterogeneous audiences through media technologies such as television, radio, newspapers, and the internet.

quizQuestions.question: A student asks a teammate to upload the final file before a deadline. Which communication function is primary?
options: Instrumental
Identity
Ritual
Aesthetic
quizQuestions.answer: Instrumental
quizQuestions.explanation: The message aims to complete a practical task, so its primary function is instrumental.

quizQuestions.question: Self-concept is best described as:
options: The reputation others form from observing your behavior
Your emotional evaluation of your personal worth
The overall mental image you hold of yourself
The impression you try to create for an audience
quizQuestions.answer: The overall mental image you hold of yourself
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-concept is the complex mental picture individuals hold of themselves, encompassing beliefs about their personality, abilities, values, and roles.

quizQuestions.question: According to Charles Cooley's 'looking-glass self,' we form our self-concept primarily through:
options: Comparing ourselves to idealized media figures
Imagining how others see and evaluate us
Our biological temperament and genetics
Formal education and academic achievement
quizQuestions.answer: Imagining how others see and evaluate us
quizQuestions.explanation: Cooley's looking-glass self theory proposes that people develop self-concept by imagining others' perceptions and judgments of them — society becomes a mirror.

quizQuestions.question: In Self-Concept & Communication, Self-esteem refers to:
options: Your confidence in completing a particular task
Your awareness of other people’s emotional states
Your beliefs about personal traits and social roles
Your evaluative judgment about your own worth
quizQuestions.answer: Your evaluative judgment about your own worth
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-esteem is the evaluative component of self-perception — how positively or negatively a person judges their own worth and competence.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Explain how repeated negative feedback from a valued peer could influence a fictional student’s self-concept through reflected appraisal. Give one supportive communication response.
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: explains that the student may internalize how the valued peer appears to judge them, without claiming this is inevitable; provides a supportive response focused on specific behavior, strengths, or opportunities to improve.
quizQuestions.explanation: Reflected appraisal involves perceived judgments from others shaping self-concept. Specific, respectful feedback can offer an alternative to a global negative label.

quizQuestions.question: Connotative meaning of a word refers to its:
options: Dictionary or literal definition
Grammatical function in a sentence
Emotional and cultural associations
Technical usage within a specialized field
quizQuestions.answer: Emotional and cultural associations
quizQuestions.explanation: Connotative meaning encompasses the emotional, cultural, and personal associations a word carries beyond its objective dictionary (denotative) definition.

quizQuestions.question: The word 'home' has a different meaning than 'house' primarily because of a difference in:
options: Connotative meaning
Denotative meaning
Grammatical structure
Abstract level
quizQuestions.answer: Connotative meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: 'Home' and 'house' share a similar denotative meaning (a dwelling) but 'home' carries warmer connotative associations of family, comfort, and belonging.

quizQuestions.question: Jargon is best described as:
options: Indirect wording that softens an unpleasant message
Specialized vocabulary shared by a group or profession
Regional expressions used in everyday informal conversations
Broad wording that leaves the intended meaning uncertain
quizQuestions.answer: Specialized vocabulary shared by a group or profession
quizQuestions.explanation: Jargon is technical or specialized vocabulary used within a profession, field, or group that may be unclear to outsiders.

quizQuestions.question: Using 'sanitation engineer' instead of 'garbage collector' is an example of:
options: Inclusive language
Euphemistic language
Abstract language
Equivocal language
quizQuestions.answer: Euphemistic language
quizQuestions.explanation: Euphemisms substitute mild or indirect expressions for words considered unpleasant or blunt, such as calling garbage collectors 'sanitation engineers.'

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of haptics?
options: Speaking more slowly to emphasize a point
Maintaining eye contact during a conversation
A handshake when greeting someone
Moving closer to a friend during a personal conversation
quizQuestions.answer: A handshake when greeting someone
quizQuestions.explanation: Haptics is the study of communication through touch; a handshake is a common form of haptic communication that conveys greeting, respect, or agreement.

quizQuestions.question: When a nonverbal cue repeats the verbal message (e.g., saying 'Turn left' and pointing left), nonverbal behavior is functioning as a:
options: Contradiction
Substitution
Complement
Repetition
quizQuestions.answer: Repetition
quizQuestions.explanation: Repetition occurs when nonverbal behavior repeats the same message as the verbal content (pointing left while saying 'turn left').

quizQuestions.question: Choosing to sit farther away during a formal interview is an example of which nonverbal channel?
options: Proxemics
Haptics
Chronemics
Artifacts
quizQuestions.answer: Proxemics
quizQuestions.explanation: Proxemics concerns how people use physical space and distance in communication.

quizQuestions.question: A speaker says “I am calm” while speaking rapidly with tense posture. The nonverbal cues primarily:
options: Repeat the words
Contradict the words
Replace the words entirely
Have no effect on meaning
quizQuestions.answer: Contradict the words
quizQuestions.explanation: The vocal and bodily cues conflict with the literal message, creating contradiction.

quizQuestions.question: Empathic listening involves:
options: Evaluating the logic of the speaker's argument
Listening only for key facts and information
Pretending to pay attention while thinking about something else
Understanding and sharing in the speaker's emotional experience
quizQuestions.answer: Understanding and sharing in the speaker's emotional experience
quizQuestions.explanation: Empathic listening requires attempting to understand and emotionally connect with the speaker's perspective and feelings, not just processing informational content.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a common listening barrier?
options: Maintaining eye contact with the speaker
Mentally preparing your response while the speaker talks
Paraphrasing what you heard to confirm understanding
Asking clarifying questions after the speaker finishes
quizQuestions.answer: Mentally preparing your response while the speaker talks
quizQuestions.explanation: Rehearsing your response while the speaker is still talking diverts cognitive resources from listening, making it a significant listening barrier.

quizQuestions.question: Open-ended questions in active listening are valuable because they:
options: Invite the speaker to elaborate and share more fully
Can be answered with a simple 'yes' or 'no'
Redirect the conversation to a new topic
Demonstrate that you already know the answer
quizQuestions.answer: Invite the speaker to elaborate and share more fully
quizQuestions.explanation: Open-ended questions (e.g., 'How did that make you feel?') invite expansive responses, encouraging the speaker to elaborate and feel genuinely heard.

quizQuestions.question: Which response best demonstrates paraphrasing?
options: “Use the earlier deadline; that should solve your problem.”
“When exactly did the teacher announce the new deadline?”
“I had a similar schedule change in my last class.”
“The change left you unsure of the deadline—is that right?”
quizQuestions.answer: “The change left you unsure of the deadline—is that right?”
quizQuestions.explanation: A paraphrase restates the speaker’s meaning and checks whether the listener understood it accurately.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Name the six HURIER listening steps and explain how interrupting before a speaker finishes can interfere with listening.
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: names Hearing, Understanding, Remembering, Interpreting, Evaluating, and Responding; explains that premature interruption can prevent hearing the complete message and lead to inaccurate understanding or evaluation.
quizQuestions.explanation: HURIER describes six listening processes. Responding is part of listening, but interrupting prematurely can block the information needed to understand and evaluate a message.

quizQuestions.question: According to Knapp's Staircase Model, the first stage of relationship development is:
options: Intensifying
Experimenting
Initiating
Integrating
quizQuestions.answer: Initiating
quizQuestions.explanation: Initiating is the first stage in Knapp's model, involving first impressions and initial contact (greeting, making oneself approachable and presentable).

quizQuestions.question: Trust is foundational to interpersonal relationships because it:
options: Eliminates the possibility of conflict
Guarantees the other person will always agree with you
Makes deeper self-disclosure and vulnerability feel safe
Is established instantly upon meeting someone
quizQuestions.answer: Makes deeper self-disclosure and vulnerability feel safe
quizQuestions.explanation: Trust creates a psychological safe space that enables partners to be vulnerable and engage in deeper self-disclosure, which is essential for relationship development.

quizQuestions.question: Why does trust often support deeper self-disclosure?
options: It reduces the perceived risk of sharing vulnerable information
It creates a duty to answer every personal question
It makes rapid disclosure the best choice for every relationship
It makes checking permission unnecessary before sharing someone’s story
quizQuestions.answer: It reduces the perceived risk of sharing vulnerable information
quizQuestions.explanation: Trust can make disclosure feel safer, although people still choose appropriate boundaries.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: In the 'experimenting' stage of knapp's model, communicators primarily engage in.
quizQuestions.answer: In the experimenting stage, communicators use small talk and safe self-disclosure to discover shared interests.
quizQuestions.explanation: Experimenting is the stage where people test possible connection through low-risk topics and limited personal disclosure.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a constructive conflict communication behavior?
options: Explaining how the other person’s character caused the disagreement
Using an I statement to describe specific behavior and its impact
Recounting past disputes to strengthen your position in this disagreement
Delaying discussion without agreeing when to return to the issue
quizQuestions.answer: Using an I statement to describe specific behavior and its impact
quizQuestions.explanation: 'I' statements describe specific behaviors and their impact without blaming ('I feel frustrated when meetings start late' vs. 'You're always inconsiderate'), making them constructive conflict tools.

quizQuestions.question: Stonewalling in conflict communication refers to:
options: Calmly presenting your perspective without interruption
Firmly restating your position until the other person agrees
Withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage
Seeking a third-party mediator to resolve the dispute
quizQuestions.answer: Withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage
quizQuestions.explanation: Stonewalling involves shutting down emotionally and withdrawing from communication — giving the 'silent treatment' — which prevents conflict resolution.

quizQuestions.question: The competing conflict style is characterized by:
options: Equal concern for self and the other party
Low concern for self and high concern for the other party
High concern for self and low concern for the other party
Low concern for both self and the other party
quizQuestions.answer: High concern for self and low concern for the other party
quizQuestions.explanation: Competing involves high assertiveness and low cooperativeness — pursuing one's own goals at the expense of the other party's needs.

quizQuestions.question: Which conflict style combines high concern for one’s own needs with high concern for the other party’s needs?
options: Collaborating
Avoiding
Accommodating
Competing
quizQuestions.answer: Collaborating
quizQuestions.explanation: Collaborating seeks a solution that addresses important concerns of both parties.

questions.question: Which model of communication depicts communication as a one-way process from sender to receiver without feedback?
options: Transactional model
Interactive model
Constructivist model
Linear model
questions.answer: Linear model
questions.explanation: The linear model (e.g., Shannon-Weaver, Lasswell) depicts communication as a one-way transmission from sender to receiver with no feedback loop.

questions.question: The relational function of communication is primarily concerned with:
options: Transmitting factual information accurately
Building and maintaining social bonds and relationships
Achieving practical task-based goals
Persuading others to change their beliefs
questions.answer: Building and maintaining social bonds and relationships
questions.explanation: The relational function of communication involves using messages to establish, develop, and maintain interpersonal connections and social relationships.

questions.question: Self-concept is primarily shaped by:
options: Biological temperament operating independently of social experience
One formative experience that fixes later self-perceptions
Feedback from significant others and comparisons with others
Academic achievement considered separately from relationships and experiences
questions.answer: Feedback from significant others and comparisons with others
questions.explanation: Self-concept develops through social interaction — feedback from parents, peers, teachers, and cultural messages — rather than any single source or biological determinism.

questions.question: Denotative meaning refers to a word’s:
options: Literal or dictionary definition
Emotional or cultural associations connected with a word
Specialized vocabulary shared within a profession or group
Wording that permits two or more different interpretations
questions.answer: Literal or dictionary definition
questions.explanation: Denotation is the direct or dictionary meaning of a word; connotation is the feeling or association that the word may carry.

questions.question: A speaker says, “I feel deeply saddened by this news,” while displaying a broad celebratory grin. Assume the grin expresses delight, rather than nervousness or an attempt to soften delivery. Relative to the expressed sadness, the grin functions to ______ the verbal message.
options: Repeat
Contradict
Complement
Regulate
questions.answer: Contradict
questions.explanation: Under the stated assumption, the delighted expression conflicts with the verbal expression of sadness and therefore contradicts it. In other contexts a smile could express nervousness or soften delivery.

questions.question: Active listening requires which of the following?
options: Planning your response while the speaker is talking
Agreeing with everything the speaker says
Interrupting to ask questions before the speaker finishes
Full concentration and engaged responding to the speaker
questions.answer: Full concentration and engaged responding to the speaker
questions.explanation: Active listening involves giving the speaker your full attention, working to understand their meaning, and responding in ways that show comprehension and engagement.

questions.question: In Knapp's Staircase Model, the 'bonding' stage is characterized by:
questions.answer: Public commitment to the relationship, such as a formal partnership, close public identity, or recognized long-term bond.
questions.explanation: In Knapp's model, bonding makes a relationship publicly recognized through formal or symbolic commitment.

questions.question: Why can an I-statement be more constructive than a blaming you-statement during conflict?
options: They describe the speaker's feelings and needs without directly blaming the other person
They make the speaker’s interpretation an established fact so the other person has no reason to disagree
They conceal an accusation behind the word I while assigning the other person full responsibility for the conflict
They remove the need to describe any specific behavior because naming an emotion settles the factual disagreement
questions.answer: They describe the speaker's feelings and needs without directly blaming the other person
questions.explanation: An I-statement describes a specific behavior, the speaker’s response, and a need or request without assigning a global negative label to the other person.

questions.question: A construction drill makes it difficult to hear a classroom presentation. This is primarily which kind of communication problem?
options: Physical noise
Feedback
Relational bonding
Intrapersonal reflection
questions.answer: Physical noise
questions.explanation: The external sound interferes with transmission and reception of the message, making it physical noise.

questions.question: Silently rehearsing what to say before asking a question is an example of which level of communication?
options: Interpersonal
Intrapersonal
Small-group
Mass communication
questions.answer: Intrapersonal
questions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication occurs within one person, including internal thought and self-talk.

questions.question: A student changes how they participate after repeated teacher and peer feedback. This most directly illustrates:
options: Reflected appraisal shaping self-concept
A fixed-ratio schedule
The denotative meaning of a word
Physical noise
questions.answer: Reflected appraisal shaping self-concept
questions.explanation: Reflected appraisal describes how perceived feedback from others can influence self-concept and later communication behavior.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes denotation from connotation?
options: Denotation is associated feeling; connotation is direct dictionary meaning
Denotation is private meaning; connotation is the shared dictionary definition
Denotation is spoken meaning; connotation is meaning conveyed through writing
Denotation is direct meaning; connotation is associated feeling or idea
questions.answer: Denotation is direct meaning; connotation is associated feeling or idea
questions.explanation: Denotation refers to a word’s direct or dictionary meaning, while connotation includes learned emotional or cultural associations.

questions.question: A listener nods while another person speaks, helping manage turn-taking. The nod primarily performs which nonverbal function?
options: Replacing every spoken word
Ending the relationship
Regulating interaction
Creating physical noise
questions.answer: Regulating interaction
questions.explanation: Nonverbal cues such as nodding can regulate conversational flow by signaling attention or inviting the speaker to continue.

questions.question: Which behavior is a listening barrier?
options: Paraphrasing and checking meaning
Asking a relevant open question
Rehearsing a rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
Summarizing the speaker’s main point
questions.answer: Rehearsing a rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
questions.explanation: Mental rehearsal divides attention and can prevent the listener from accurately understanding the speaker’s full message.

questions.question: The 'looking-glass self' concept explains self-concept development through:
options: Biological and genetic inheritance
How we imagine others perceive and judge us
Formal academic assessment and feedback
Early childhood unconscious memory formation
questions.answer: How we imagine others perceive and judge us
questions.explanation: Cooley's looking-glass self proposes that self-concept forms as we imagine others' views of us and internalize those imagined evaluations as self-perception.

questions.question: In the communication process, noise refers to:
options: The receiver’s verbal or nonverbal response to the sender’s original message
The medium used to carry a message from one communicator to another
Interference with transmitting or interpreting a message
The content expressed through the words or symbols selected by the sender
questions.answer: Interference with transmitting or interpreting a message
questions.explanation: Noise interferes with a message’s transmission or interpretation; feedback is a response, a channel is a medium, and the message is the communicated content.

questions.question: The instrumental function of communication serves to:
options: Maintain social bonds through friendly exchanges and emotional support
Express personal identity through descriptions of values and experiences
Accomplish practical tasks and achieve tangible goals
Offer enjoyment through stories, jokes, and playful exchanges
questions.answer: Accomplish practical tasks and achieve tangible goals
questions.explanation: The instrumental function involves using communication to get things done — making requests, giving instructions, completing transactions, and achieving practical objectives.

questions.question: Proxemics is the study of how people use:
options: Vocal pitch, volume, and speaking rate during face-to-face conversations
Physical space and distance in communication
Gesture and body movement to convey meaning
Time and timing as communicative resources
questions.answer: Physical space and distance in communication
questions.explanation: Proxemics (Hall) examines how physical distance — intimate, personal, social, and public zones — functions communicatively in different relationships and contexts.

questions.question: The primary difference between hearing and listening is:
options: Hearing interprets meaning; listening detects vibrations in the ear
Hearing requires deliberate attention; listening happens automatically
Hearing uses spoken words; listening relies on nonverbal signals
Hearing detects sound; listening involves attention and interpreting meaning
questions.answer: Hearing detects sound; listening involves attention and interpreting meaning
questions.explanation: Hearing is the passive, physiological reception of sound; listening is the active, cognitive process of attending to and making sense of the sounds received.

questions.question: Which pattern most directly supports trust in an interpersonal relationship?
options: Following through consistently and clarifying misunderstandings honestly
Offering reassurance before checking whether a promise is realistic
Withholding concerns so the other person never feels challenged
Sharing a friend’s private story to demonstrate closeness to others
questions.answer: Following through consistently and clarifying misunderstandings honestly
questions.explanation: Trust grows when communication and behavior are reliable and misunderstandings are addressed openly and respectfully.

questions.question: Explain the difference between denotative and connotative meaning, using one word in a school-safe example.
questions.answer: A valid response states that denotation is the word’s direct or dictionary meaning, while connotation is the feeling or association the word carries, and shows both meanings in a specific example.
questions.explanation: The distinction explains why two accurate words can shape an audience differently.

questions.question: A message intended as a joke is read as insulting because the text channel removed tone and facial cues. Which concept best explains the breakdown?
options: Channel and noise
Bonding stage
Collaborating style
Instrumental function
questions.answer: Channel and noise
questions.explanation: A text channel carries fewer nonverbal cues, and semantic or psychological noise can change interpretation.

questions.question: The accommodating conflict style is characterized by:
options: High concern for self and low concern for others
Equal concern for self and others
Low concern for both self and others
Low concern for self and high concern for others
questions.answer: Low concern for self and high concern for others
questions.explanation: Accommodating involves setting aside one's own needs and concerns to satisfy the other party — low assertiveness but high cooperativeness.

questions.question: Which revision is the clearest I-statement?
options: I felt left out when the schedule changed without a message; can we agree on an update process?
I feel that you are completely irresponsible whenever a schedule changes, and I expect you to admit that this whole problem is your fault.
Everyone knows you caused this.
Whatever—you decide.
questions.answer: I felt left out when the schedule changed without a message; can we agree on an update process?
questions.explanation: The revision describes a specific behavior and impact, then makes a concrete request without labeling the other person.

questions.question: When interpreting a crossed-arm posture, the most responsible conclusion is:
options: Crossed arms alone are enough to conclude the person is defensive
The setting and other cues are needed before interpreting the posture
The posture conveys more reliable meaning than the person’s spoken explanation
The meaning learned in one culture can be applied across cultures
questions.answer: The setting and other cues are needed before interpreting the posture
questions.explanation: Nonverbal cues are ambiguous; setting, culture, baseline behavior, and other cues affect interpretation.

questions.question: Pseudo-conflict is best resolved by:
options: Compromising over resources before checking what each person meant
Asking a mediator to choose a winner without clarifying meanings
Clarifying the misunderstanding that created the apparent conflict
Postponing the discussion while leaving each interpretation unexamined
questions.answer: Clarifying the misunderstanding that created the apparent conflict
questions.explanation: Since pseudo-conflict is based on misperception or misunderstanding rather than real incompatibility, clarifying the misunderstanding typically dissolves the conflict.

questions.question: Which listener response is a perception check?
options: “You seem upset, so I will move the deadline without discussing it.”
“I have had deadline changes too; here is what worked for me.”
“You are concerned about the changed deadline, not the task. Is that right?”
“Let us discuss the task instructions first and return to your concern later.”
questions.answer: “You are concerned about the changed deadline, not the task. Is that right?”
questions.explanation: A perception check states a tentative interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm or correct it.

questions.question: A classmate says, “Fine, do whatever you want,” while looking away and speaking quietly. Explain two plausible interpretations and state what question could clarify the message.
questions.answer: A valid response recognizes that the words and nonverbal cues may conflict, offers two context-sensitive interpretations, and proposes a neutral clarification such as, “I may be reading mixed signals—are you comfortable with this plan?”
questions.explanation: Responsible interpretation avoids treating one nonverbal cue as proof and uses feedback to check meaning.

questions.question: Which response best demonstrates empathic listening?
options: Offering a solution before asking how the speaker feels
Paraphrasing the concern and emotion, then checking your understanding
Reassuring the speaker that the situation is probably not serious
Relating your own similar experience before hearing the full account
questions.answer: Paraphrasing the concern and emotion, then checking your understanding
questions.explanation: Empathic listening attends to content and feeling while allowing the speaker to correct the listener’s interpretation.

questions.question: Why can clear boundaries support a trusting relationship?
options: They clarify what information and behavior each person feels comfortable with
They establish rules that eliminate the need to revisit changing expectations
They show that closer relationships require disclosing increasingly private information
They allow one person to determine the other’s disclosure choices
questions.answer: They clarify what information and behavior each person feels comfortable with
questions.explanation: Clear boundaries support voluntary, appropriate disclosure and reduce uncertainty about expectations; trust does not require sharing everything.

questions.question: In Knapp’s model, experimenting is most associated with:
options: Making a public commitment that formally defines the relationship
Using small talk and low-risk disclosure to explore common ground
Increasing distance by reducing conversation about previously shared interests
Developing a shared identity through more frequent and personal interaction
questions.answer: Using small talk and low-risk disclosure to explore common ground
questions.explanation: Experimenting uses safe topics and limited disclosure to explore possible connection.

questions.question: Which behavior is most likely to escalate a conflict?
options: Asking how the revised plan affects the other person’s priorities
Inviting the other person to clarify what caused their concern
Summarizing shared goals before discussing the remaining points of disagreement
Making an absolute accusation such as “You always ruin everything”
questions.answer: Making an absolute accusation such as “You always ruin everything”
questions.explanation: Global blame and absolutes attack identity rather than address a specific behavior or need.

questions.question: Which response best uses collaborative conflict management?
options: “My deadline is firm; please adjust your plan to meet it.”
“I will accept your deadline even though my concern remains unresolved.”
“Let us postpone this discussion without setting a time to return.”
“Let us identify both priorities and test a plan addressing each.”
questions.answer: “Let us identify both priorities and test a plan addressing each.”
questions.explanation: Collaboration combines concern for one’s own needs with concern for the other party’s needs.

questions.question: Which of the following communication behaviors would best demonstrate active listening?
options: Nodding, making eye contact, and paraphrasing what the speaker said
Looking at your phone while the speaker talks
Immediately sharing your own related experience when the speaker pauses
Mentally preparing counterarguments while the speaker is talking
questions.answer: Nodding, making eye contact, and paraphrasing what the speaker said
questions.explanation: Active listening behaviors include attentive nonverbal signals (nodding, eye contact) and verbal feedback (paraphrasing) that demonstrate comprehension and genuine engagement.

questions.question: Rewrite this blaming message as a constructive conflict message: “You never do your part.” Include an observation, impact or feeling, and a specific request.
questions.answer: One valid response is: “The last two assigned sections were not uploaded by the agreed deadline, and I felt stressed because I could not assemble the final file. Can we assign owners and confirm uploads by 6 p.m.?”
questions.explanation: Constructive messages describe observable behavior, explain impact, and make a specific request without global labels.
